content: Infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and the progression to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) represent a global pandemic that has impacted millions of individuals worldwide. While significant research and clinical efforts have been directed toward prevention and cure strategies, the quality of life for those living with HIV/AIDS has received comparatively less attention. Massage therapy has been proposed as a potential intervention to enhance quality of life and may also positively influence immune function by mitigating stress. The purpose of this systematic review was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of massage therapy in improving quality of life, alleviating pain, and influencing immune system parameters in individuals living with HIV/AIDS. A comprehensive search strategy was employed to identify relevant studies, incorporating terms related to HIV/AIDS, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), massage therapy, and associated outcome measures. Searches were conducted across multiple electronic databases in November 2008, including the Cochrane Group Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others. Additionally, conference abstracts, proceedings, and reference lists from relevant journals were reviewed. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. Studies were selected based on specific criteria: they had to be RCTs involving participants of any age with HIV/AIDS at any stage of the disease, and the intervention had to include massage therapy aimed at improving quality of life, immune function, pain reduction, or other physiological or psychological outcomes. Two reviewers independently identified eligible studies and extracted data, while two additional reviewers assessed the risk of bias. Data and bias assessments were entered into RevMan software, and meta-analyses were conducted when appropriate. Out of twelve identified papers, four studies met the inclusion criteria, while the remaining eight were excluded due to methodological issues. The included studies were clinically diverse, involving participants across various age groups (children, adolescents, and adults) and disease stages (from early HIV to late-stage AIDS). The settings ranged from community-based care to palliative care. Outcome measures included assessments of quality of life and immunological function. The studies were judged to have a moderate risk of bias, primarily due to incomplete reporting. Regarding quality of life, the studies indicated that massage therapy, when combined with other interventions such as meditation and stress reduction techniques, was more effective than massage therapy alone or the other interventions alone. Significant improvements were observed in domains such as reduced self-reported use of healthcare resources, enhanced self-perceived spiritual quality of life, and overall quality of life scores. One study reported positive changes in immune function, specifically increases in CD4+ cell counts and natural killer cell counts, associated with massage therapy. However, another study found no significant differences in immune parameters between individuals receiving massage therapy and control groups. Adverse effects or harms related to massage therapy were not well-documented. In conclusion, there is some evidence to suggest that massage therapy can improve the quality of life for people living with HIV/AIDS, particularly when combined with other stress-management interventions. Additionally, massage therapy may have a beneficial impact on certain immunological parameters. However, the included trials were small and carried a moderate risk of bias. Larger, rigorously designed studies are needed to confirm these findings and provide stronger recommendations for the use of massage therapy in this population.
